about: Messtechnik (376.045) and the Messtechnik-Labor (376.046) at TU Wien, after the course book of Schrüfer et al. (2012), Elektrische Messtechnik, 10th edition, and the lab script of Schitter (2015), winter term 2015/16. Equation numbers and pages are the book's printed ones, read in its text layer on 1 Nov 2026; the lab script's tasks are cited by number and its printed page (Seite). The book's worked examples (Beispiele) and its Table 5.8 are the practice questions where they exist; the rest were worked by hand from the book's equations and say so. tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes every answer with the core and fails if they disagree. Spectrum analysis (the DFT, windows, leakage) is the Signals and Systems lab's; three-phase power the Power engineering lab's; Bode plots the Automation lab's.

labs.title: Repeated readings and their mean
labs.idea: Readings of one quantity scatter; their mean is uncertain by only s/√N, and with few readings Student's factor t widens the interval.

equations.note: the mean of N readings
the empirical standard deviation of one reading, its standard uncertainty
the standard deviation of the mean
the result with a coverage factor, normal readings
Student's factor for few readings, Table 1.6

practice.question: Ten readings of a voltage: 6.7, 6.4, 6.3, 6.6, 6.5, 6.7, 6.5, 6.3, 6.6, 6.4 V. What is the standard uncertainty of their mean?
practice.solution: Mean 65.0 V/10 = 6.5 V. The squared deviations add to 0.20 V², so s = √(0.20/9) = 0.15 V and s/√N = 0.15/√10 = 0.047 V: the result is (6.5 ± 0.047) V at 68.3 %.
practice.source: Schrüfer et al. (2012), Beispiel 1.3, Table 1.5, p. 40

practice.question: Five readings scatter with s = 0.15 V. How wide is the 95.5 % half-interval of their mean, with Student's factor?
practice.solution: Table 1.6 gives t = 2.98 for N = 5 at 95.5 %. u = t · s/√N = 2.98 · 0.15/√5 = 0.200 V, against 0.134 V with the normal factor 2.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 1.83 and Table 1.6, p. 44

labs.title: Propagation of uncertainty
labs.idea: A result computed from several measured quantities inherits their errors: known systematic ones add with their sensitivities, independent random ones add as squares, Gauss's law.
labs.lecture: Schrüfer et al. (2012), sections 1.3.3 and 1.3.6, pp. 35–43; Schitter (2015), task 2.5

equations.note: a known systematic error carried through the model, linearised

equations.eq: Δy/y = Σ αᵢ · Δxᵢ/xᵢ for y = Π aᵢ xᵢ^αᵢ
equations.tex: \frac{\Delta y}{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_i \frac{\Delta x_i}{x_i} \qquad \text{for } y = a_1 x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots a_n x_n^{\alpha_n}
equations.note: for products of powers the relative errors add, weighted by the exponents
Gauss's law for independent inputs (1821)
the lab script's model: the uncertainty of P from those of I and Φ
every contribution with the same sign: an upper bound

practice.question: Full package g₃ = 600 g with s₃ = 9 g, empty package g₁ = 80 g with s₁ = 5 g. What is the standard deviation of the contents g₂ = g₃ − g₁?
practice.solution: Both partial derivatives have magnitude 1, so s₂ = √(9² + 5²) g = √106 g = 10.3 g. 95 of 100 packages hold (520 ± 20.6) g.
practice.source: Schrüfer et al. (2012), Beispiel 1.4, p. 43

practice.question: Relative errors ΔU/U = −0.011 and ΔR/R = −0.031. What is the relative error of P = U²/R (as a fraction)?
practice.solution: P = U² · R⁻¹, so ΔP/P = 2 · (−0.011) − 1 · (−0.031) = +0.009: the power reads 0.9 % high and can be corrected.
practice.source: Schrüfer et al. (2012), Beispiel 1.2, p. 36

labs.title: The meter loads the circuit
labs.idea: A voltmeter draws current and forms a divider with the source's resistance; an ammeter adds its resistance to the loop. Each reads true only when it is far larger, or far smaller, than the circuit.
labs.lecture: Schrüfer et al. (2012), section 2.1.2, pp. 90–93; Schitter (2015), tasks 1.1.1–1.1.2

equations.note: a voltmeter across a source with internal resistance Ri
an ammeter in a loop of resistance R
equations.ref: eq. 2.24, p. 89, as IM = UL/(Ri + RM)

equations.eq: Ri = RM when the reading halves
equations.note: how to find a meter's or a source's resistance
the shunt that extends a current range
the series resistor that extends a voltage range

practice.question: A movement of 400 Ω reads full scale at 0.2 mA. Which shunt makes it read 1 mA full scale?
practice.source: Schrüfer et al. (2012), Beispiel 2.1, p. 91

practice.question: That shunted movement (400 Ω ‖ 100 Ω, 1 mA full scale) is to read 100 mV full scale. Which series resistor does it need?
practice.solution: The movement drops 1 mA · 80 Ω = 80 mV (eq. 2.32), so Rv = 100 mV/1 mA − 80 Ω = 20 Ω.
practice.source: Schrüfer et al. (2012), eqs. 2.32–2.35, pp. 92–93

practice.question: A 10 V source with 100 kΩ internal resistance is read by a voltmeter of 10 MΩ. What does it show?
practice.source: Worked by hand, after Schitter (2015), task 1.1.1 (U = 10 V, 100 kΩ)

labs.title: Resistance from voltage and current
labs.idea: Measured with an ammeter and a voltmeter, a resistance reads too high when the voltmeter also sees the ammeter's drop and too low when the ammeter also carries the voltmeter's current; each circuit suits one end of the scale.
labs.law: Rx = U/I − RA or Rx = U/(I − U/RV)
labs.lecture: Schrüfer et al. (2012), section 3.1.1, pp. 195–196; Schitter (2015), task 1.1.3

equations.note: current-correct circuit (Bild 3.1 a), for large resistances
voltage-correct circuit (Bild 3.1 b), for small resistances
where both raw errors are equal, to first order
comparison with a reference resistor in series avoids the error

practice.question: 100 Ω measured current-correct with an ammeter of 1 Ω. What does U/I give before correction?
practice.solution: The voltmeter sees Rx and RA in series: U/I = Rx + RA = 101 Ω, 1 % high. Eq. 3.1 subtracts RA.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 3.1, after Schitter (2015), task 1.1.3

practice.question: With RA = 1 Ω and RV = 1 MΩ, above which resistance is the current-correct circuit the better one?
practice.solution: Current-correct errs by RA/Rx, voltage-correct by about Rx/RV. They are equal at Rx = √(RA·RV) = √(10⁶) Ω = 1 kΩ.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eqs. 3.1–3.2

labs.title: Mean, rectified mean and RMS
labs.idea: A rectifier meter measures the rectified mean and multiplies by 1.11, the form factor of a sine; for any other waveform it reads wrong, while a true-RMS meter does not.
labs.law: form factor = RMS/rectified mean = 1.11 for a sine
labs.lecture: Schrüfer et al. (2012), section 2.1.3, pp. 95–99; Schitter (2015), tasks 1.2.2–1.2.3

equations.note: the linear mean, the DC part, what a moving coil shows
the rectified mean
the RMS value
for a sine

equations.eq: crest factor = û/U = 1.41; form factor = U/|ū| = 1.11
equations.note: for a sine

practice.question: A rectifier multimeter calibrated for sines measures a square wave of 1 V peak. What does it show?
practice.solution: The rectified mean of a ±1 V square wave is 1 V; the scale multiplies by 1.11, so it shows 1.11 V, while the RMS value is 1 V: 11 % high.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eqs. 2.37–2.44 and p. 98

practice.question: The same meter on a triangle wave: what is its relative error (as a fraction)?
practice.solution: A triangle of peak û has rectified mean û/2 and RMS û/√3. The meter shows 1.1107 · 0.5 û = 0.5554 û against 0.5774 û: −3.8 %.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eqs. 2.37–2.39

labs.title: Compensating a 10 : 1 probe
labs.idea: The probe's resistor and trimmer capacitor and the scope's input form a divider that is the same at every frequency only when both halves have the same time constant; a square wave shows whether they do.
labs.lecture: Schrüfer et al. (2012), section 2.2.2, pp. 115–116; Schitter (2015), task 1.2.1

equations.note: the frequency-compensated divider
flat in frequency

equations.tex: R_\mathrm{T} C_\mathrm{T} = R_\mathrm{E} C_\mathrm{E}^{*}, \qquad C_\mathrm{E}^{*} = C_\mathrm{E} + C_\mathrm{K}
equations.note: the probe's condition, the cable's capacitance included
at an edge the capacitors divide
once settled the resistors divide
how fast it settles between the two, from the node equation

practice.question: A scope input of 1 MΩ with 100 pF including the cable, a probe resistor of 9 MΩ. Which trimmer capacitance compensates it?
practice.solution: CT = RE · CE*/RT = 1 MΩ · 100 pF/9 MΩ = 11.1 pF. Type 11.1p.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 2.100

practice.question: The same probe trimmed to 8 pF: what fraction of a step appears at the edge?
practice.solution: CT/(CT + CE*) = 8/108 = 0.074, less than the 0.1 it settles to: under-compensated, the corners round off.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eqs. 2.101–2.102

labs.title: The Wheatstone bridge
labs.idea: Balanced, the bridge measures a resistance as a ratio, whatever the supply; deflected, its diagonal voltage follows a small change, bent for one active arm and straight for opposite changes in one divider or for four active arms.
labs.lecture: Schrüfer et al. (2012), sections 3.3 and 3.11, pp. 199–205 and 238–239; Schitter (2015), tasks 3.1.1 and 3.3

equations.eq: Ud = U₃ − U₁ = U₀ (R₂R₃ − R₁R₄)/((R₁ + R₂)(R₃ + R₄))
equations.note: the diagonal voltage, U₁ across R₁, U₃ across R₃

equations.tex: R_2 R_3 = R_1 R_4 \;\Rightarrow\; R_2 = \frac{R_1 R_4}{R_3}
equations.note: balance, and the unknown from it
the quarter bridge
half bridge with opposite changes in one divider, and full bridge: exact

equations.eq: Ri = R₁ ‖ R₂ + R₃ ‖ R₄; IM = Ud/(Ri + RM)
equations.note: the bridge as a source loaded by a meter

equations.eq: ΔR/R₀ = K ε; σ = F/A = E ε
equations.note: a strain gauge on a loaded bar

practice.question: A steel bar of 10 cm² carries 100 kN; E = 2·10¹¹ N/m². A gauge with K = 2 sits in a 5 V quarter bridge. What is the diagonal voltage?
practice.solution: σ = F/A = 10⁸ N/m², ε = σ/E = 5·10⁻⁴, ΔR/R₀ = Kε = 10⁻³, Ud = U₀/4 · 10⁻³ = 1.25 mV.
practice.source: Schrüfer et al. (2012), Beispiel 3.2, p. 239

practice.question: R₁ = 1 kΩ, R₃ = 2 kΩ and R₄ = 4.7 kΩ balance the bridge. What is the unknown R₂?
practice.solution: R₂ = R₁R₄/R₃ = 1 kΩ · 4.7 kΩ/2 kΩ = 2.35 kΩ.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 3.14

practice.question: A full bridge on 10 V, every gauge changing by 0.2 %. What is the diagonal voltage?
practice.solution: Ud = U₀ · ΔR/R₀ = 10 V · 0.002 = 20 mV, four times the quarter bridge and exactly linear.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), Bild 3.9 h

labs.title: Active power and the wattmeter
labs.idea: Instantaneous power swings at twice the line frequency about its mean U·I·cos φ, which the wattmeter's pointer settles on; the meter's own paths take power, and where the voltage path is clamped decides which.
labs.lecture: Schrüfer et al. (2012), section 2.1.4, pp. 101–104; Schitter (2015), task 2.8

equations.eq: α = k I₁ I₂ cos φ
equations.note: the electrodynamic movement averages the product of its coils' currents

equations.eq: P = U I cos φ; Q = U I sin φ; S = U I
equations.tex: P = U I \cos\varphi \qquad Q = U I \sin\varphi \qquad S = U I
equations.note: active, reactive and apparent power
the source's power splits between the load and the meter

equations.eq: error = UV²/RU (at the load); IV² RI (at the source)
equations.tex: \frac{U_\mathrm{V}^2}{R_U} \;\text{(at the load)} \qquad I_\mathrm{V}^2 R_I \;\text{(at the source)}
equations.note: the meter's own consumption in the two connections of Bild 2.26 a, b

equations.eq: p(t) = U I [cos φ − cos(2ωt + φ)]
equations.note: the instantaneous power

practice.question: 230 V, 2 A, the current lagging by 30°. What active power does the wattmeter show?
practice.solution: P = U I cos φ = 230 V · 2 A · cos 30° = 398.4 W; Q = 230 var, S = 460 VA.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 2.56

practice.question: With the voltage path of 20 kΩ clamped at the load, which error does 230 V at the load add to the reading?
practice.solution: The current path carries the voltage path's current too, so the meter adds U²/RU = 230²/20 000 W = 2.645 W.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 2.51 and Bild 2.26 a

labs.title: The seismic vibration sensor
labs.idea: A mass on a spring inside a shaking housing lags behind it: far above its natural frequency it stands still and the pick-up reads displacement, far below it follows and reads acceleration.

equations.note: the mass's motion xa relative to the housing, the housing's xe
the standard form, T = 1/ω₀ = √(m/c), D = w/(2√(cm))

practice.question: A seismic mass of 0.1 kg hangs on a spring of 1000 N/m. What is its natural frequency?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 7.112

practice.question: With D = 1, what fraction of the housing's displacement does the sensor read at its natural frequency?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 7.115

labs.title: Counting frequency and period
labs.idea: A counter opens a gate and counts edges; the count is uncertain by one, so counting the signal for a gate T resolves 1/T, and timing one period with a clock f₀ resolves fx²/f₀.
labs.law: fx = Nx/T; Nx = f₀ Tx; ±1 count

equations.note: a time interval or period counted in clock periods; ±1 count
a frequency counted in a gate of known length
the gate made by counting N₀ clock periods
where both modes resolve alike: 1/T = fx²/f₀

practice.question: A counter with a 1 s gate counts a 100.3143 kHz signal. What frequency does it give?
practice.solution: Nx = 100 314 edges in 1 s; a 4-digit counter in overflow shows 0314. The result is 100 314 Hz ± 1 Hz.
practice.source: Schrüfer et al. (2012), Table 5.8, p. 299

practice.question: A 50 Hz signal is timed over one period with a 10 MHz clock. How fine is the resolution in frequency?
practice.solution: Nx = f₀/fx = 200 000 counts, ±1, so a relative 5·10⁻⁶ and Δf = fx²/f₀ = 0.25 mHz, against 1 Hz for a 1 s gate.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eqs. 5.7 and 5.9

practice.question: With a 10 MHz clock and a 1 s gate, below which frequency is period measurement the finer?
practice.solution: 1/T = fx²/f₀ gives fx = √(f₀/T) = √(10⁷) Hz = 3.16 kHz.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eqs. 5.7 and 5.9

labs.title: Flash, successive approximation, dual slope
labs.idea: A flash converter compares with every level at once; successive approximation weighs one bit per step; the dual slope integrates the input for a fixed time and times the reference's way back, so R, C and the clock cancel.

equations.note: the parallel (flash) converter, thermometer code to Gray code

equations.eq: ūx Na/f = U₀ Nx/f ⇒ Nx = (Na/U₀) ūx

practice.question: An 8-bit successive-approximation converter on 0–10 V converts 6.3 V. What code (as a decimal number) does it give?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), section 6.2.5

practice.question: A dual-slope converter runs down for Na = 1000 clock periods; U₀ = 2 V; the input is 1.234 V. What does it count?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Schrüfer et al. (2012), eq. 6.16

practice.question: How many comparators does an 8-bit flash converter need?
practice.solution: 2⁸ = 256 ranges need 255 comparators; the 3-bit converter of Bild 6.4 has seven.
